title: The daily inner buzz of Shakespeare
author: David James
summary: English teacher David James responds to James Marriott's plan to learn a short Shakespeare passage every week by describing how he asks his own Year 9 class to memorise speeches from Othello. He opens by pairing Prospero's "Our revels now are ended" with Macbeth's "Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow," arguing that both compare life to a performance but reach opposite emotional conclusions. He then argues that memorised poetry is a lifelong boon, an inner voice of wisdom that returns at the moment it is needed, rather than a party trick. To support the point he describes using Gemini to turn a passage by Professor John Carey into slides in seconds, and notes that the class took only two minutes to learn Iago's warning about jealousy. He observes that the lines stick because of how they are said as well as what is said, in the grammar of eight consecutive monosyllables. The post is a short, practical case for retrieval of language by heart.
points: Memorising passages is presented not as a feat of memory but as building a private store of language that outlasts the moment it was learned.
Pairing Prospero and Macbeth shows how the same insight about transience can produce despair or wonder depending on language, structure and tone.
A small incentive, releasing the class from homework if everyone is word-perfect, is used to concentrate pupils' minds on learning speeches by heart.
The sound of the verse, such as eight consecutive monosyllables in Iago's warning, is part of why lines are remembered.
AI is used here as a fast preparation aid for slides, while the real learning still happens in a two-minute recitation task.
quotes: I am currently teaching Othello to a Year 9 class and have asked them to learn certain passages by heart
once learned, Shakespeare (or any good poetry) can be a lifelong boon: an inner voice of wisdom you can carry with you and use when you need it most.
A line learned at thirteen has a way of returning when you least expect it, and when you most need it.
You don’t consult it so much as find it already there, waiting to say what you couldn’t quite say yourself.
It isn’t a party trick or a feat of memory: it’s a small, private store of language that outlasts the moment you learned it.
They will remember the lines not only because of what is said, but because of how it is said.
Gemini made the slides in seconds; the class took two minutes, and kept the lines for the rest of their lives.
